# Depth and texture

<a id="dep-01"></a>
## DEP-01 - Use shadows to show elevation of floating elements

Shadows help users see what floats above the page and what they can click or move; a dropdown without a shadow blends into the page.

- **Source:** PDF 50 (printed 49), 51 (printed 50)
- **Applies when:** Dropdowns, menus, popovers and other overlays.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Depth and texture (shadows, outlines, varying background colours) guide eyes and actions, create hierarchy and make interactive elements noticeable.
- Shadows help users figure out what they can click or move and look better than flat design.
- A dropdown with a subtle shadow appears to float above the page and is easier to focus on.

**Mistake:** Overlay panel with no shadow or separation from the page beneath.  
**Effect:** The panel merges with page content.

**Correction:** Add a subtle shadow (see DEP-03/DEP-04 for its quality).  
**Why it works:** Elevation separates layers.

**Observable checks:**
- Do dropdowns, popovers and menus have a shadow or another clear separation from the underlying page?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [DEP-03](13-depth.md#dep-03), [DEP-05](13-depth.md#dep-05), [CON-02](06-contrast.md#con-02)

<a id="dep-02"></a>
## DEP-02 - Add shadows to elements over dynamic backgrounds

Controls and labels overlaid on maps, photos or other complex, variable backgrounds need shadows so they don't get lost.

- **Source:** PDF 51 (printed 50)
- **Applies when:** Map overlays, floating controls on media.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Overlapping elements can get lost on complex backgrounds; a map label and zoom controls without shadows risk blending into the variable background.

**Mistake:** Flat map labels/zoom buttons with no shadow.  
**Effect:** Controls blend into the map.

**Correction:** Give overlays a shadow.  
**Why it works:** Keeps them distinguishable whatever is underneath.

**Observable checks:**
- Are there controls overlaid on maps, images or video without shadow or solid backing?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [DEP-01](13-depth.md#dep-01), [CON-03](06-contrast.md#con-03)

<a id="dep-03"></a>
## DEP-03 - Use soft shadows

Harsh, dark, all-around shadows look overbearing and unprofessional; prefer lighter shadows offset downward that blend with the background.

- **Source:** PDF 52 (printed 51)
- **Applies when:** Any shadowed element.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Too harsh or too distinct shadows look overbearing and unprofessional; opt for softer shadows that blend with the background.
- Incorrect: X0 Y0 blur 48 colour #9F9F9F. Correct: X0 Y12 blur 48 colour #E9E9E9.

**Mistake:** Dark grey, zero-offset, all-around shadow.  
**Effect:** Heavy, dirty-looking halo.

**Correction:** Lighter shadow colour with a downward Y offset.  
**Why it works:** Mimics soft, natural top lighting.

**Observable checks:**
- Inspect box-shadow: zero offset with dark colour (e.g. darker than about #C0C0C0 on white) suggests a harsh shadow.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The values are the source's examples, not universal settings.

**Related:** [DEP-04](13-depth.md#dep-04), [DEP-05](13-depth.md#dep-05)

<a id="dep-04"></a>
## DEP-04 - Tint shadows to match the background colour

On coloured backgrounds, a pure grey or black shadow clashes; tint the shadow with the background hue.

- **Source:** PDF 53 (printed 52), 54 (printed 53)
- **Applies when:** Shadowed elements on non-white, coloured backgrounds.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Matching the shadow colour to the background improves cohesiveness.
- On light purple: incorrect grey X0 Y19 blur 48 #C7C7C7; correct purple-tinted X0 Y19 blur 56 #CFC9DD.
- On cream/yellow: incorrect X0 Y20 blur 60 #D8D8D8; correct X0 Y12 blur 48 #E3D5B2.
- The source's advice: never go back to pure grey or black shadows on coloured backgrounds.

**Mistake:** Neutral grey shadow on a coloured surface.  
**Effect:** Jarring; breaks visual harmony.

**Correction:** Use a darker, desaturated tint of the background colour as the shadow colour.  
**Why it works:** The shadow reads as part of the surface's lighting.

**Observable checks:**
- On coloured backgrounds, is the shadow colour neutral grey/black (zero saturation)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [DEP-03](13-depth.md#dep-03)

<a id="dep-05"></a>
## DEP-05 - Define a shadow system

Create a rule book for shadows that matches the brand: at least soft, medium and strong levels, each tied to element types.

- **Source:** PDF 55 (printed 54), 56 (printed 55)
- **Applies when:** Design systems and any product using elevation.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- A shadow system ensures shadows are used the same way every time and fit the brand (simple vs flashy).
- At least three styles: soft for slightly lifted elements (buttons, small cards, thumbnails); medium for focus elements (modals, pop-ups), a bit darker and more spread; strong for elements that must really stand out (dropdown menus, important alerts).
- Variations are possible, e.g. a medium shadow with a different tint for warnings, or a very subtle shadow for text boxes.

**Mistake:** Ad-hoc shadow values per component.  
**Effect:** Inconsistent depth cues.

**Correction:** Define elevation tokens (e.g. xs to 2xl; at minimum soft/medium/strong) and assign them by component type.  
**Why it works:** Depth becomes meaningful and predictable.

**Observable checks:**
- Count distinct box-shadow values in the codebase; do they map to a small set of named levels?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The xs to 2xl scale figure gives no values.

**Related:** [DEP-01](13-depth.md#dep-01), [DEP-03](13-depth.md#dep-03), [CNS-01](11-consistency.md#cns-01)

<a id="dep-06"></a>
## DEP-06 - Separate sections with subtle background layers or outlines

A light grey page with white cards, or thin light outlines, creates structure; an all-white dashboard can look too plain.

- **Source:** PDF 56 (printed 55), 57 (printed 56), 58 (printed 57)
- **Applies when:** Information-dense UIs such as dashboards (but not limited to them).

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Background colour and outlines create depth subtly; this is especially valuable for dashboards.
- Pure white background and elements can work but may look too plain; a light grey background with white cards gives a layered, structured look and helps users focus on sections.
- Alternatively, thin outlines segment areas, guide the eye and create natural divisions.

**Mistake:** Sidebar, stat blocks and charts all on one undifferentiated white surface.  
**Effect:** No visual sections; harder to parse.

**Correction:** Light neutral page background with white cards, or thin light outlines around cards.  
**Why it works:** Layers communicate grouping.

**Observable checks:**
- Are distinct dashboard sections separated by background, outline or spacing?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [DEP-07](13-depth.md#dep-07), [DEP-08](13-depth.md#dep-08), [WS-01](08-whitespace.md#ws-01)

<a id="dep-07"></a>
## DEP-07 - Don't overdo borders

Too many borders and background bands clutter a UI; separate sections with whitespace and colour instead, using borders sparingly.

- **Source:** PDF 59 (printed 58), 60 (printed 59)
- **Applies when:** Modals, lists, forms, tables.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Overusing borders clutters and looks busy, confusing or outdated; multiple borders and several background colours per section cause visual overload.
- The corrected modal uses no borders and relies on colour and generous whitespace to separate results and buttons; borders are effective when used sparingly and intentionally.

**Mistake:** Header divider, bordered search band, dividers on every row and a bordered footer band in one modal.  
**Effect:** Visual noise that detracts from content.

**Correction:** Remove most borders; use spacing and a filled search field to separate.  
**Why it works:** Fewer lines mean less noise and the content leads.

**Observable checks:**
- Count border lines in a component: are there borders that duplicate a separation already made by spacing or background?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [DEP-08](13-depth.md#dep-08), [DEP-06](13-depth.md#dep-06)

<a id="dep-08"></a>
## DEP-08 - Keep borders thin and light (break the rule only deliberately)

Thick, dark borders overpower content and feel heavy; use subtle lines. A thick border can work if it is soft and serves a deliberate style.

- **Source:** PDF 60 (printed 59), 61 (printed 60), 62 (printed 61)
- **Applies when:** Tables, buttons, input and container outlines.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Thick, dark, prominent borders overpower content and look heavy and outdated; thin light dividers define sections without stealing the spotlight. Less is often more.
- Sometimes it's okay to break the rule: a bold 10px border that is soft, semi-transparent and light can suit a specific style or brand, as long as balance is maintained and it is done deliberately.

**Mistake:** Dark heavy row dividers and dark outlined buttons in a table.  
**Effect:** Heavy and hard on the eyes.

**Correction:** Thin, light-grey dividers and light outlines.  
**Why it works:** Lines do their job without drawing attention.

**Observable checks:**
- Are border colours dark (near text colour) or widths above about 1-2px without a deliberate style reason?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- A thick border is acceptable when soft (light, semi-transparent) and deliberate for the brand (source example: 10px soft light-blue border on a search box).

**Related:** [DEP-07](13-depth.md#dep-07)

<a id="dep-09"></a>
## DEP-09 - Use glassmorphism only when it fits and stays readable

Frosted-glass effects add depth and sophistication, but they must suit the brand and never compromise readability or accessibility.

- **Source:** PDF 63 (printed 62), 64 (printed 63), 65 (printed 64)
- **Applies when:** Translucent panels over imagery.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Glassmorphism is not one-size-fits-all: decide whether it fits the brand and benefits users (e.g. a SaaS product may find it modern; a luxury cosmetics brand may prefer traditional minimalism).
- A flat dark player is fine; a glass player over a dark photo can work; glass over a light, misty background compromises readability and accessibility.
- Trends should never come at the expense of readability and accessibility.

**Mistake:** Light translucent panel with white text over a light background.  
**Effect:** Low contrast text and controls; hard to read.

**Correction:** Use glass only over sufficiently dark/contrasting backgrounds with a tint, or use a solid surface.  
**Why it works:** Translucency inherits the background's luminance.

**Observable checks:**
- Measure text contrast on glass panels against the lightest region behind them.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [CON-03](06-contrast.md#con-03), [TYP-09](15-typography.md#typ-09)
